Description

Rocky Mountain Conservancy is excited to offer two seasonal environmental education fellowships that give current students and recent college graduates the opportunity to serve in a national park while exploring careers in environmental education and the nonprofit sector. Each fellowship is unique and tailored to the individual’s skills, interests, and career goals. This is your chance to live and learn in Rocky Mountain National Park, while supporting the Conservancy's efforts in education, stewardship, and conservation!  


2027 Fellowship dates: April 14th, 2027 - October 20th, 2027


First review of applications: December 1, 2026


These fellowships are designed for highly motivated individuals passionate about outreach and education. Successful fellows thrive in a self-directed environment, where there is a balance between Conservancy-assigned and fellow-selected projects. Each fellowship includes: 

On-the-job training and experience in a variety of environmental education programs and settings 
Opportunities to develop and lead programs individually and in partnership with both Rocky Mountain Conservancy (RMC) and Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP) teams 
Housing and utilities are provided at no cost along with a stipend for living expenses 
Professional development and networking opportunities with park and nonprofit staff 

As a fellow, you will have the opportunity to build real-world experience in both the nonprofit and public sectors. Our fellowship will help you develop: 

A deep understanding of the Conservancy’s work and partnerships 
Knowledge of the region’s natural and cultural history 
Skills in program planning and delivery, participant communication, and outreach 
A professional portfolio of education and outreach work products 

Required Skills: 

Dedication to environmental and outdoor education, with the ability to lead programs for children, teens, and adults 
Adept communication skills, both written and spoken, for diverse audiences and using various media 
Strong problem-solving skills, and the ability to organize ideas and information quickly 
Demonstrated ability to independently manage long-term projects and complete assignments on time 
Desire and ability to work both collaboratively and independently 
Computer experience with Canva and the Microsoft Office suite, including Word and Outlook, preferred 
Enthusiasm, a warm disposition, and the ability to handle the stresses of working outdoors with diverse groups of program participants 

Responsibilities: 

Develop and lead interactive outdoor programs (i.e. pop-up table talks, and educational bus tours) for diverse audiences, including families, youth, and adults 
Support expert-led Field Institute programs
Assist with development, planning, and implementation for a range of Conservancy programs 
Support RMNP education and interpretation programs, such as school field trips and Jr. Ranger programs 
Create outreach and promotional materials for Conservancy programs 
Establish and maintain positive working relationships with RMNP staff and volunteers, as well as with other Conservancy partners, program participants, and community members 
Assist Conservancy and park staff with outreach events 
Drive and/or ride in Conservancy-owned vehicles, including the Conservancy’s 15-passenger buses 
Each position averages 30-40 hours per week, with schedules that vary throughout the fellowship. A full 6-month commitment is required.  

Fellows are provided with housing (including all utilities) for the duration of their fellowship. Shared housing units are located near Conservancy headquarters in Estes Park, CO, in units operated by Rocky Mountain National Park. Fellows also receive a living stipend of $450/week (paid as $900 every two weeks). Fellows must be eligible to work in the USA and must pass a background check. 


It is recommended that the candidate be actively pursuing or have recently completed a degree program in environmental education, general education, communication, outdoor recreation/tourism, natural resource management, or similar. In addition, experience volunteering or working with nonprofit organizations and an interest in public outreach and conservation is desired. 


Visit us online to learn more: https://rmconservancy.org/work-with-us/environmental-education-fellowships/

How to Apply
To apply, email your resume, cover letter, and at least three professional references (including phone numbers and
email addresses) to [email removed] In the subject line, specify whether you’re applying for the Outdoor Education Fellowship or the Environmental Education Fellowship.

Katie Colson

Description
The Biology Department at East Tennessee State University (ETSU) is seeking a motivated masters student starting fall 2027 to join Dr. Ryan Stephens' lab (https://ryanbstephens.wordpress.com). The Stephens’ lab focuses on understanding ecological interactions and community dynamics with a strong focus on trophic ecology of mammals and their consumption and dispersal of fungal spores and seeds. Graduate students will have the opportunity to work on projects involving both field research and lab-based studies, contributing to our understanding of ecological interactions and the functional roles that small mammals play in forested ecosystems. There is room for project development depending on the student’s interest with main research foci including 1) truffle-mammal interactions and the dispersal of fungal spores, 2) seed selection and dispersal by small mammals, and 3) trophic niche dynamics of small mammals.
 Position Requirements:
A bachelor’s degree in biology, ecology, environmental science, or a related field.
Previous research experience in ecology, natural resources, biology, or a related discipline is preferred.
·       Experience with field data collection, especially small mammal live trapping or taking forest compositional measurements is preferred but not required.
A valid US drivers license (or the ability to get one).
 Opportunities and Support:
The position is based at ETSU in Johnson City Tennessee and is available beginning August 2027. The ideal candidate will be able to start field data collection in May of 2027. Field work will take place in the Blue Ridge Mountains of East Tennessee. The Masters student will have support for 2 years including a tuition waver and stipend ($12,200) along with summer salary guaranteed in 2027.
 To apply, please email ([email removed]) your CV, statement of research interests (2 pages max), and contact information for three references. Include “Graduate student application” along with your last name in the email title. Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until the position is filled. To receive full consideration please apply before November 1, 2026. Please refer to https://www.etsu.edu/cas/biology/academics/ms_bio.php for information about the Biology M.S. program.

Description
Description: A fully funded master’s assistantship is available in Oklahoma State University’s Department of Natural Resource Ecology & Management (NREM), co-advised by Dr. Scott Loss (NREM) and Dr. Bruce Noden (OSU Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology). The graduate student will address research questions related to the role of birds in carrying ticks and tick-borne pathogens in the U.S. Great Plains, a region with a high incidence of several tick-borne diseases and where birds are known to be important carriers of ticks. The MS student will lead research that includes: (1) field work to mist-net wild birds—primarily passerines (songbirds) and near-passerines (e.g., cuckoos and woodpeckers)—to search them for ticks and collect blood samples, and (2) laboratory work to test ticks and bird blood samples for the presence of bacterial pathogens. The student will also have the opportunity to work with Drs. Noden and Loss to identify and refine specific research questions related to birds, ticks, and disease ecology. This project will expand knowledge about the ecology of tick borne diseases, including the role of birds as tick bloodmeal hosts and reservoir hosts for tick-borne pathogens. The student will complete coursework and labwork on the OSU campus in Stillwater, with fieldwork in parks and greenspaces in and around Stillwater.

Ideally, the graduate student will be available by March or April of 2027 to begin planning and leading the first season of fieldwork in spring/summer of 2027 before matriculating in classes at OSU starting in August 2027. However, there is some flexibility in this schedule and we are willing to consider alternative start dates (e.g., beginning coursework as early as January 2027 or beginning coursework in August 2027 and completing the first field season in the following spring/summer). Regardless of start date, full funding will be available for 2.5 years (5 academic semesters plus 2 field seasons). Funding will be through a research assistantship, but the student may also have an opportunity to TA for one or more semesters (course TA assignment to be determined, but the student may be able to TA in Dr. Loss’s field ecology course or in NREM’s ornithology course). A stipend of $2,083/month ($25,000/yr) will be provided along with full tuition waiver and health insurance at $20/month.

Required qualifications: Applicants must possess: an undergraduate degree in Natural Resource Management, Wildlife Ecology/Management, Ecology, Biology, Entomology, or a related field; a strong work ethic and sense of self-motivation; an ability to work both independently and collegially with others; strong written and oral communication skills; strong quantitative analysis skills and/or an ability to quickly learn and apply quantitative skills; and an interest in disease ecology and wildlife ecology and management. Applicants also must be able to identify bird species of the central United States, and have experience with fieldwork focused on birds, including mist netting and banding of wild birds (as the graduate student will lead bird netting as a subpermittee under Dr. Loss’s master banding permit). However, this experience does not need to include previous independent leadership of bird mist-netting efforts, and we will provide support and needed training to ensure the student is ready to work independently.

Preferred qualifications: Candidates with one or several of the following skills and experiences will be particularly competitive: past independent leadership of bird mist-netting and banding activities; experience conducting, presenting, and/or publishing mentored research; experience coordinating and supervising research projects; experience independently conducting statistical and/or spatial analyses using programs such as R and ArcGIS.

To Apply: Please send applications to Dr. Scott Loss ([email removed]) by Nov 20, 2026. Applications should consist of a single zip file or merged pdf file (with the file name format: Your Last Name_BirdTickMS) that includes: (1) a cover letter outlining how you meet required and preferred qualifications, and noting what your preferred start date is, (2) a CV, and (3) contact information for three references. We are committed to fostering an environment where diversity of background and thought is accepted and encouraged, and we encourage all interested people to apply despite preconceived notions of their own experience as it relates to this project’s objectives.

About the Loss and Noden Labs: Dr. Loss’s lab leads a wide range of research projects in natural resource ecology and management, with emphases on global change ecology, disease ecology, biodiversity, and the conservation of migratory birds. Dr. Noden’s lab focuses on the effect of ecological and environmental factors on arthropod vector populations and the pathogens they transmit, including work with ticks, mosquitoes, and fleas. Drs. Loss and Noden have collaborated collegially for more than a decade to mentor graduate students conducting research at the interface of disease ecology, avian ecology, and natural resource management. For more information about our labs, see:

Scott Loss’s Lab: https://scottrloss.wixsite.com/losslab 
Bruce Noden’s Lab: https://experts.okstate.edu/bruce.noden 

About Oklahoma and OSU: Oklahoma is one of the most ecologically diverse states, with ecosystems ranging from forested mountains in the east to mesas and canyons in the west, and including some of the largest remaining tracts of prairies in the world. Recreational opportunities abound, with national forests, grasslands, and wildlife refuges within 2-3 hours of Stillwater, where OSU is located. Stillwater is 1 hour from both Oklahoma City and Tulsa, which have additional opportunities for recreation, sporting events, music, the arts, restaurants, etc.

OSU is a land-grant institution with an enrollment of ~25,000 students and is located on the ancestral lands of the Kickapoo, Osage, Kiowa, and Quapaw peoples. Indigenous people from other Native nations also reside here, many of whom were forcibly removed from their ancestral lands. They all contribute to the history and current vitality of our region. The Department of Natural Resource Ecology and Management is part of the Division of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Resources and conducts interdisciplinary research, instruction, and extension education to address the sustainable management and conservation of the wildlife, forest, rangeland, and fishery resources of Oklahoma and beyond. The Department is a source of cutting-edge research, quality instruction, and effective outreach to students, landowners, managers, and public agencies.

Any offer of employment is contingent on the university’s verification of credentials and other information required by law and/or university policies, including but not limited to a criminal background check. Oklahoma State University, as an equal opportunity employer, complies with all applicable federal and state laws regarding non-discrimination and affirmative action. Oklahoma State University is committed to a policy of equal opportunity for all individuals and does not discriminate based on race, religion, age, sex, color, national origin, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity/expression, disability, or veteran status with regard to employment, educational programs and activities, and/or admissions.

Position Description: Chronic wasting disease (CWD) is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy of cervids.  The disease is 100% fatal, yet genetic variants are known to affect transmission of CWD and longevity of affected animals.  None provide complete resistance, unlike in domestic sheep, where prion gene alleles provide complete resistance to scrapie.  To date, most studies of genetic variation associated with CWD susceptibility in free-ranging mule and white-tailed deer have been done in areas far from the core of the species’ ranges.  The central-marginal hypothesis predicts that more genetic variation should occur near the core of a species range than at the periphery. Therefore, a survey of other geographic regions may reveal additional genetic variation. 
 In Texas, CWD is present in free-ranging deer in the Panhandle–Trans-Pecos regions and in Medina County of South Texas.  The goal of this research is to better understand genetic variation in free-ranging Texas mule and white-tailed deer, especially genetic variants associated with CWD susceptibility.  The results of this study will have direct input into applied management for the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department as well as the USDA.  The student will work closely with state, federal, and private entities in collaboration with scientists from the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute, have the opportunity to present research at regional and national scientific conferences and to stakeholders, and will be expected to publish their results in peer-reviewed journals. 
 Location: Successful applicant will pursue a M.S. in Rangeland and Wildlife Management at Texas A&M University-Kingsville (TAMUK).  The Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute is a privately endowed research unit embedded in the university, with 28 scientists and about 65 M.S. and Ph.D. students. TAMUK has an enrollment of about 7,000 and is located in Kingsville, a city of about 26,000 in the south coastal plains.  Kingsville is surrounded by the historic King Ranch and is about 40 miles south of Corpus Christi.  Field portion of the research (sample collection) will be conducted on private lands in Texas. 
 Qualifications Required:  B.S. degree in ecology, wildlife science, biology, or related fields. Competitive applicants will have a strong work ethic, good verbal and written communication skills, quantitative skills, and the ability to work independently as well as a productive member of a research team.  Students should have a minimum 3.0 GPA.

Preferred: Background and interest in large mammals or disease ecology.  Familiarity with DNA extraction and analysis of DNA sequence data or quantitative or programming skills (R, Python, etc.) would be helpful but not required. 

Texas law requires that males age 18 through 25 show proof of compliance with Federal Selective Service law to be eligible for employment. 
Selected candidate must pass a pre-employment background investigation to be hired for this position.

 Start Date: Negotiable, prefer January 2027. 
 Application Deadline: Begin reviewing applications as received and will continue until a suitable candidate is selected. 
 To Apply: Application packet must consist of 1) cover letter stating interests and career goals, 2) resume or CV, 3) academic transcripts and 4) contact information for 3 references.

*Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis and applications may close before the deadline.

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP), within the Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP), located in Durham, North Carolina. You will receive training in the Research Triangle Park, NC campus and may be required to travel to Washington, DC once a year for debriefings.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: You will gain experience in data management, analysis, and technical skills for coordinated research and informatics efforts supporting EDSP. The appointment will focus on data science activities related to toxicological and targeted bioactivity screening data as part of the US EPA Toxicity Forecaster (ToxCast) program, including model maintenance, productionizing research endpoints, development of R packages, software development, database curation, and quality evaluation of in vitro chemical screening data. Research activities may include acquiring domain knowledge in toxicology and chemistry; wrangling heterogeneous source formats into standard templates; conducting data analysis and curation using controlled vocabularies; performing database scripting; managing code libraries and documentation; identifying and correcting bugs; conducting user acceptance testing; developing automated tools for processing large volumes of data; and applying innovative data science solutions to support hazard identification, screening prioritization, risk assessment, and regulatory decision-making. You may also gain experience with the evaluations of the predictivity and precision of new approach methods (NAMs) relative to traditional animal testing.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn how to: 

Design and implement reusable and scalable techniques for data management
Organize or transform data in databases to support scientific analyses 
Analyze data quality according to specified criteria
Write scripts and functions in R to support data migration and data curation software tools
Develop and collaborate with others to evolve scientific applications into production level tools
Create and interact with RESTful APIs to support scientific efforts
Create proof of concept projects and adapting/maintaining code from other researchers
Other research activities may include:

Gain experience being a part of an interdisciplinary team of software developers, data scientists, and subject-matter experts.
Develop skills in creating clear, effective data visualizations to communicate results to stakeholders and technical audiences.
Build proficiency in thoroughly documenting data, code, analytical methods, and procedures in accordance with EPA quality-assurance procedures, supporting transparency and reproducibility.
Strengthen technical writing skills by drafting reports that describe complex datasets, data-processing methods, and data-manipulation procedures.
Prepare internal reports and memoranda that communicate analytical research and findings for use by EPA scientists.
Develop scientific communication experience through opportunities to present research at scientific conferences and contribute to peer-reviewed manuscripts.
Mentor(s): The mentors for this opportunity are Madison Feshuk ([email removed]) and Scott Lynn ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: December 1, 2026. All start dates are flexible and vary depending on numerous factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

EPA Security Clearance: Completion of a successful background investigation by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is required for an applicant to be on-boarded at EPA.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and EPA. Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5 year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received a bachelor's or master's degree in one of the relevant fields (toxicology, environmental science, cell/molecular biology, biochemistry, or a closely related field of study). Degree must have been received within the past five years.

Training or courses in statistics or computer programming
Domain knowledge of biology or toxicology processes desired
Strong reading comprehension skills and experience logically interpreting pieces of information from a variety of data source types
Experience programming in the R language
Experience utilizing R packages for code development and data analysis, such as devtools and tidyverse, desired
Experience writing CRAN compliant R packages and/or functions desired
Experience with relational databases, such as MySQL, PostGreSQL, or others

Description
*Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity focused on the development of novel detection methods for foodborne pathogenic bacteria is available at the USDA, Agricultural Research Service, Eastern Regional Research Center, Characterization and Interventions for Foodborne Pathogens (CIFP) Research Unit in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The mission of the CIFP research unit is to investigate multiple areas of safety-related problems associated with contamination of food by bacterial pathogens and includes: stress response, evolution/mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, intervention techniques, and rapid detection & identification. The research project in this subgroup focuses on the stress responses for specific foodborne pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes). Analysis is typically complicated by the complex nature of food matrices and the frequent need to develop virulence assays using different mammalian cell lines.

During the appointment, you will assist in research and development focused on one or more advanced areas of interest (e.g., molecular microbiology and biochemistry). This research will complement your academic education with the application of:

BSL2 pathogen handling
Genome sequencing, transcriptomics
Bioinformatic analysis, Computational biology
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn about food-safety research focused on bacterial contamination and foodborne pathogens.
Develop knowledge of stress-response mechanisms in pathogens such as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Gain experience investigating pathogen evolution and mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence.
Learn how food-matrix complexity affects the detection, characterization, and analysis of foodborne bacteria.
Build skills in developing and conducting virulence assays using mammalian cell lines.
Strengthen laboratory research, experimental-design, and data-analysis skills relevant to microbial food-safety studies.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Andrew Gehring ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: December 1, 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The anticipated stipend is $6,857/mo with an allowance of $691.68/mo for health insurance. 

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received or be currently pursuing a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Preferred skills:

Sterile technique
Knowledge of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
DNA/RNA isolation
Basic molecular techniques

Description
Dr. Nicki Nimlos, Principal Investigator of The RangeLab, is recruiting a fully funded Ph.D. graduate student to develop and lead a rangeland and livestock monitoring program in Wyoming. The program will include (but is not limited to) vegetation, soil, grazing, and livestock behavioral monitoring through traditional and emerging monitoring techniques. The research project will involve working closely with producers and other stakeholders, and the student will have the ability to develop additional research questions. Engagement with producer and rangeland management organizations will be highly encouraged as part of the position. Other expectations include regular meetings with Dr. Nimlos, attending college seminars and activities, submitting research to peer-reviewed journals and Extension bulletins, and presenting at scientific conferences and stakeholder meetings.  
 The student will be housed in the Department of Ecosystem Science and Management at the University of Wyoming in Laramie, Wyoming, and will pursue a graduate degree in Rangeland Ecology and Watershed Management. The position will begin in the summer of 2027 on campus in Laramie, WY. The student is expected to be on campus during the academic semester and in the field during the summer.  

Qualifications: Students with a BS and/or MS degree in Rangeland Management, Ranch Management, Natural Resources, Botany, Ecology, Environmental Science or a related field and a competitive GPA (>3.0) are encouraged to apply. Experience with rangeland monitoring, field data collection, and statistical analysis is preferred. The student must be physically able to perform fieldwork with little supervision, able to work well with research technicians, and have strong verbal, written, and computational skills. Applicants with previous experience and coursework in rangeland management and animal science are encouraged to apply. Proficiency in spoken/written English, a valid US driver’s license, and the ability to pass Wyoming DMV check are needed.  
 Specifics: The student will be supported by an assistantship including academic and summer salary, tuition and fees, and health insurance based on the current UW rates (https://www.uwyo.edu/uwgrad/enrolled-students/financial-assistance/assistantship-funding.html). The student will be supported by a combination of research assistantships (RA) and teaching assistantships (TA) for at least 3 years. Funding beyond the third year is contingent on the availability of additional funding. The student will be advised by Dr. Nimlos. This project requires travel across Wyoming which will include overnight stays and substantial time in a vehicle.  
 Application: To apply, please fill out the following form: https://forms.gle/SNSVDyBZunWCLK7g8  
 Applications received prior to November 23, 2026 will receive priority in review, but the position will remain open until filled. Upon hire, candidates must apply to the University of Wyoming Graduate Admissions program (http://www.uwyo.edu/uwgrad/prospective/applying/index.html).  
 Hiring statement: All qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, disability, or status as a protected veteran. In compliance with the ADA Amendments Act (ADAAA), if you have a disability and would like to request an accommodation to apply for a position, please contact us at 307-766-2377 or email [email removed].  
 About Laramie: The University of Wyoming is located in Laramie, a town of 32,000 in the heart of the Rocky Mountain West. The state of Wyoming continues to invest in its university, helping to make it a leader in academics, research and outreach. The university has state-of-the-art facilities in many areas and the community provides the advantages of a major university. 
 Located in a high mountain valley near the Colorado border, Laramie offers both outstanding recreational opportunities and close proximity to Colorado’s Front Range, a bustling group of metropolitan cities including Denver, Boulder, and Fort Collins. This beautiful mountain landscape offers outdoor enjoyment in all seasons, with over 300 days of sunshine annually. For more information about the region, please visit http://visitlaramie.org/.

The Smith BIRDS Lab (https://smithbirdslab.com/) is recruiting graduate students (MS or PhD) for fall 2027 or spring 2028. The lab has a wide range of research interests but focuses its core on farming for people and nature. Research on co-managing farmlands for avian conservation and ecosystem service provisioning is a large portion of the lab’s efforts. We currently seek students to work on projects related to (1) ecosystem services and disservices resulting from songbird nestbox use, (2) conservation outcomes of using songbird nestboxes on farms, and (3) optimal prairie strip implementation and design for birds and ecosystem services. While birds are a large interest of the lab, we also work with insects, particularly in the context of integrated pest management. Current projects focus on insect pest control services provided by birds and food safety externalities resulting from birds, and these lines of work are priorities to continue. We also are pursing lines of work related to avian reproductive success and parasite burden.

Applicants must have graduated with a bachelor’s degree in ecology or related field by June 2027. Description
Graduate Research Assistant in Rangeland Vegetation Ecology at MSU
Position Summary
This graduate research assistantship will support a Master of Science in Animal and Range Sciences, with an emphasis in Range Science, at Montana State University (MSU) in Bozeman. The student will work under the supervision of Dr. Georgia Harrison, Rangeland Ecologist in the Department of Animal and Range Sciences, on a thesis focused on rangeland vegetation ecology and field-based vegetation monitoring. The research will evaluate how grazing management and livestock use influence plant community composition, vegetation structure, and forage availability across Montana rangelands, in collaboration with an interdisciplinary team investigating vegetation, livestock production, and soil properties. The position provides a stipend of $33,000 per year, starting in January 2027 through May or August 2029. Tuition is not included, but opportunities to pursue scholarships and other tuition support may be available.
The position begins in January 2027 and continues through May or August 2029, with academic-year appointments (full-time, >6 credits) and summer appointments (part-time, <6 credits). The student will work collaboratively with an interdisciplinary research team investigating relationships among vegetation, livestock production, and soil properties. The position will involve substantial fieldwork, including plant identification, vegetation sampling, biomass collection, and repeated monitoring of permanent plots. The student will also organize and analyze ecological data, interpret results, and communicate findings to scientific and management audiences.
Responsibilities
• Conduct seasonal vegetation field sampling at rangeland research sites and cooperating ranches, including in remote locations and variable weather conditions.
• Identify grasses, forbs, shrubs, and other rangeland plant species.
• Measure plant community composition and vegetation structure, including cover, height, and canopy gaps.
• Collect and process biomass samples to estimate forage availability and functional-group biomass.
• Evaluate vegetation responses to grazing management, livestock distribution, and environmental conditions.
• Use GPS and GIS tools to locate sampling sites and manage spatial data.
• Manage, quality-check, and analyze field data using R, spreadsheets, GIS, and other appropriate tools.
• Collaborate on vegetation, livestock, and soil sampling with the broader research team.
• Contribute to peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, research reports, and extension outreach.


Qualifications
Required
• Bachelor's degree in rangeland ecology, range science, plant ecology, ecology, natural resources, environmental science, or a related field.
• Eligibility for admission to a master's program at Montana State University in the Department of Animal and Range Sciences
• Ability and willingness to conduct physically demanding fieldwork in remote rangeland environments and variable weather conditions.
• Ability to work independently and collaboratively, follow standardized sampling protocols, and maintain accurate field records.
Preferred
• Experience identifying grasses, forbs, and shrubs, particularly western rangeland species.
• Experience with vegetation monitoring, plant community sampling, biomass clipping, or ecological field research.
• Familiarity with rangeland monitoring methods, such as line-point intercept, canopy gap measurements, nested frequency, or similar techniques.
• Experience with R, GIS, spreadsheets, or other tools for ecological data management and analysis.
• Experience safely operating ATVs or other off-road vehicles and towing trailers.
• Interest in grazing ecology, rangeland management, and applied research conducted in collaboration with land managers.
How to Apply
Interested applicants should email Dr. Georgia Harrison at [email removed] with the subject line “MS Graduate Research Assistant – Rangeland Vegetation Ecology (Jan 2027).”
Please include a one-page cover letter describing your interest in the position, relevant experience, and career goals along with a current curriculum vitae or résumé. Applications will be reviewed as received. Applicants are encouraged to describe their experience with plant identification, rangeland vegetation monitoring, ecological fieldwork, and data analysis, as applicable.

Contact
Georgia Harrison
406-994-5558
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

 Description 

The Holmes lab at Southern Illinois University is recruiting a PhD student for a fully funded, 5-year research assistantship. Application deadline is December 30. Salary is $25,700 per year. The research should focus on the impacts of roads on natural systems in the eastern hardwood forest, ideally with the possibility of improving conservation practices for state and federal threatened and endangered species. Contact Iris Holmes ([email removed]) for more information. 

Duties 

The student will conduct sampling for threatened and endangered bats at new construction sites (approximately 5-10 per year). Sampling will involve laying out tarps to collect fecal samples, preserving samples in the field, extracting DNA from the samples in the lab, and using Sanger sequencing to barcode the samples to identify bat species. A report on species IDs must be completed within 15 days of sample collection. 

Research focus 

In addition to bat monitoring, the student will develop a research program as part of the new Roadside Ecology Center at SIU. The taxon focus is flexible, but the research should apply to conservation of threatened and endangered species or to conservation of Illinois habitats. Possible research areas could include (but are not limited to) validating eDNA methods for detection of vertebrates or invertebrates from water samples, using eDNA methods to study connectivity in aquatic systems, developing analytical methods to account for imperfect detection in metapopulation or niche models, quantifying road impacts on animal diets, or determining the impact of construction- or road-related stressors on animal microbiomes or parasite infection rates. 

Desired qualifications 

Bachelor’s degree in biology or a related field 

Master’s degree or 1 or more years of work experience 

Experience with molecular lab work and/or field work 

Interest in landscape management or conservation policy

Description
The Lab of Conservation Ecology at Northern Arizona University (Drs. Clare Aslan and Sara Souther) is recruiting three graduate students to start in Fall 2027. All three positions focus on applied ecology that produces data-driven management guidance for Southwestern landscapes.

1. Culturally informed restoration of Madrean oak woodlands (MS or PhD; advisors Souther & Aslan)
Funded by an Emory Oak Collaborative Tribal Restoration Initiative (EOCTRI) Fellowship: a 2-year project for an MS student or a 4-year project for a PhD student. The student will work on Emory oak (Quercus emoryi), a foundational and culturally significant tree, within EOCTRI. EOCTRI is a long-term partnership among Western Apache Nations, land managers, and NAU that works to sustain the tradition of Apache acorn harvest. The student will also contribute to the NSF DISES project linking oak population dynamics to Indigenous land stewardship, drought, and fire. Responsibilities include managing a statewide demographic census of Emory oak, coordinating treatment monitoring, and evaluating restoration effectiveness.
Details: https://ses-nau.org/student-opportunities/find-an-advisor/sara-souther/

2. Sustainable rangeland management on the Colorado Plateau (MS; advisor Aslan)
Funded by a 2-year Olajos-Goslow MS Fellowship. The student will quantify the effects of long-term experimental grazing on biodiversity, examine disturbance resilience on rangelands, and assess restoration practices.

3. Biodiversity and resilience in the southeastern Arizona borderlands (MS; advisor Aslan)
Funded by a 2-year Olajos-Goslow MS Fellowship. The student will study how endangered and culturally important plants respond to drought and fire, including fuels-treatment effectiveness, demography of focal species, and biodiversity across disturbance-severity gradients.
Details for #2 and #3: https://ses-nau.org/student-opportunities/find-an-advisor/clare-aslan/

Ideal candidates have demonstrated fieldwork experience, an interest in applied ecology, a commitment to working with diverse communities and partners, a desire to build data-analysis skills, independence, and strong writing skills.

Description
The Vennum Lab at Boise State University seeks a motivated graduate student to join the M.S. in Raptor Biology program and contribute to the Butte Valley Raptor Research Project, a long-term research and monitoring effort on Swainson's Hawks (Buteo swainsoni) in northern California.
 
For decades, this project has tracked known-age individuals through mark-resight and annual nest monitoring, building a multi-faceted, long-term dataset on reproductive success and demography. This foundation supports questions about life-history evolution and the conservation of this long-distance migrant. We are also working to expand the program with developing research on nestling physiology and telemetry-based movement data to examine how hawks use agricultural landscapes. Together, this growing dataset and its planned expansion open the door to interdisciplinary thesis questions spanning demography, life history, physiology, and movement ecology.
 
The student's thesis question will be developed collaboratively, drawing on the project's existing data and research directions while leaving room for the student's own interests and ideas. Expectations for data use and authorship will be outlined in a lab mentoring agreement.
 
The M.S. program begins in Fall 2027. There may be an opportunity to begin graduate research and on-site fieldwork earlier, around April 2027.
 Funding
This position is supported by a Teaching Assistantship, which includes:
 Tuition 
Healthcare benefits
$22,000 starting annual stipend

The Raptor Research Center (RRC) at Boise State has supported graduate education, research and technical assistance to researchers since 1987. Learn more about the RRC here website.
 Project Description
The position is part of the Butte Valley Raptor Research Project, a long-term effort studying raptor ecology, movement, and habitat use in northern California. The project combines field surveys, nest monitoring, banding, and habitat data collection to support conservation and management on working landscapes.

The student’s primary field duties will include searching for and monitoring nests, resighting color-banded birds, and banding nestlings. Under appropriate supervision and permits, the student may also have opportunities to climb trees and gain experience handling and banding multiple raptor species. A field vehicle and fuel are provided for project work.

Fieldwork is based in Macdoel, California, in the Butte Valley region. This rural, high-elevation basin includes grasslands, agricultural fields, and views of the surrounding mountains. Students should be comfortable living in a remote area with limited urban amenities. Because much of this work takes place on both public and private lands, the student will build working relationships with landowners and represent the project professionally. 

The student will work with a collaborative team from Boise State University, the SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry, and Avian Behavior Conservancy. The student will have opportunities to present at scientific conferences and publish their thesis research. 

Qualifications
Applicants do not need to have experience in all of these areas to apply. We are particularly interested in students who are excited to learn new approaches, develop their skills through graduate research, and can work well with project collaborators. We especially encourage applications from first-generation college students and people from groups underrepresented in wildlife biology. 
 
Required Qualifications
 Bachelor’s degree in biology, wildlife, ecology, or a related field, completed before the April 2027 start date.
Strong interest in avian ecology, population ecology, and/or demography
Strong organizational skills and attention to detail
Ability to work both independently and collaboratively in a research team
Ability to work outdoors for extended periods in variable weather conditions, including heat, dust, and sun exposure. This position requires regular fieldwork in remote and rugged environments.
A valid driver’s license

Preferred Qualifications

Experience with statistical data analysis or coding (e.g., R, Python, JavaScript)
Strong written and oral communication skills
Enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research bridging demography, physiology, and conservation
A positive attitude and commitment to contributing to a respectful, inclusive, and collaborative lab environment

Application Instructions
Interested candidates should send the following materials to Dr. Chris Vennum at chrisvennum [at] boisestate.edu by November 13th, 2026:
 Cover Letter (1 page) – Describe your research interests, relevant experience and skills (see required and preferred qualifications), and why you are interested in this project and joining the Raptor Research Center at Boise State University.
Curriculum Vitae (CV) – Please include your GPA, relevant research or field experience, and contact information for three references.
 Submit all application materials in a single PDF file named:  LastName_FirstName_2026_SWHA_MS.pdf  

Questions about the position or project are welcomed by email.
Contact
Chris Vennum
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Assistant Professor of Biology - Tenure Track

The University of Central Missouri’s Biology Program is seeking applicants for a tenure-track position of Assistant Professor of Biology to begin in Fall 2027.  This position includes teaching, research, and service. Teaching responsibilities will include a course at all levels of departmental curriculum, including but not limited to a general education course, a major’s course in population, conservation, or evolutionary genetics, and a graduate course in the candidate’s area of expertise. The development of an externally funded, collaborative research program involving undergraduate and graduate students is expected.  The candidate will also be expected to help academically advise biology students, supervise internships, serve on university committees, and participate in curriculum development as needed. The successful candidate will complement existing departmental strengths and address genetic/genomic research questions fundamental to population or evolutionary biology.  The candidate will have access to renovated teaching spaces for both didactic or active style instruction and can extend the classroom through research in recently remodeled laboratory spaces, a registered herbarium, a wildlife research lab, a prairie research plot, and the UCM Pertle Springs Wildlife and Recreation Area.  

Faculty within the College of Health, Science, and Technology at University of Central Missouri support the university’s mission of providing student-centered, quality education and are committed to the success of students.  This includes quality teaching, advising, collegiality and communication.  In addition, faculty provide service to their program, department and university, engage in research, scholarship, and professional development activities. During contractual employment, faculty members are expected to be available to assist, engage, and respond to students, colleagues, departmental, college, and institutional needs.  

Examples of Duties

Teaching - The primary responsibility of the faculty is quality teaching in their respective content areas, regardless of delivery format. This entails adequate preparation for courses, effective course design and instruction, and fair and timely evaluation/feedback of student progress. To ensure quality teaching, faculty must be committed to the success of students as well as ongoing assessment of curriculum and of student learning.

Organize courses to facilitate quality student engagement and high impact practices.

Active membership and/or office holding in professional organizations at the local/state/regional/national level.
Service - An expectation of a professional faculty member is to serve the department, college, and university community.

Engaging in committee work that will advance the department/college/institution.
Assisting with student recruitment.
Participating in graduation and convocation ceremonies.

This implies an understanding of the communication hierarchy within departments, colleges, and administrative levels. Timely communication with students supports other faculty responsibilities (teaching, advising). 
Cultivate a collegial atmosphere when interacting with other faculty/staff within their own department, the college and the university.

Description
MS POSITION IN CONSERVATION SCIENCES
Revitalizing Hunting, Fishing and Trapping in White Earth Using Participatory GIS

Project Summary
Hunting, fishing and trapping are essential components of the culture and livelihoods of tribal nations throughout Minnesota. However, participation in these activities have been steadily decreasing in many communities. This is concerning because wild meat and fish are critical to tribal protein sovereignty and security. The Umana Laboratory (PIs: Christopher Shaffer and Marissa Milstein) in the Department of Fisheries, Wildlife and Conservation at the University of Minnesota – Twin Cities is recruiting a Masters Student in the Conservation Sciences program for a participatory mapping project focused on revitalizing hunting, fishing and trapping in the White Earth Nation. This research is in partnership White Earth Natural Resources and seeks to 1) identify the barriers to participation in these activities and 2) develop a community-based GIS for education, traditional knowledge exchange and increasing management capacity.

Requirements & Qualifications
• BS or BA in wildlife, ecology, anthropology or related field
• Basic proficiency with GIS and strong interest in further developing GIS skills
• Interest in mixed-methods research including qualitative and quantitative methods
• Strong work ethic; excellent oral and written communication skills; high attention to detail; the ability to work independently with tribal partners; and deep respect for Indigenous sovereignty; dedication to cultivating respectful partnerships with Indigenous communities in research
• A positive attitude and the personality to work/live amicably with others will also be an advantage

Research Project: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will help conduct research toward the improvement of the malting quality of barley lines produced in US breeding programs. USGS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), located at Bozeman, Montana.

The USGS mission is to monitor, analyze, and predict current and evolving dynamics of complex human and natural Earth-system interactions and to deliver actionable intelligence at scales and timeframes relevant to decision makers. As the Nation's largest water, earth, and biological science and civilian mapping agency, USGS collects, monitors, analyzes, and provides science about natural resource conditions, issues, and problems. 

Scientists at the Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center (NOROCK) in Bozeman, Montana conduct research on five general science research themes: 1) Biosurveillance of Biological Threats, 2) Wildlife Disease, 3) Fisheries and Water Resources, 4) Wildlife and Terrestrial Habitat, and 5) Cryosphere Science. 

Research Project: This is an opportunity to train with the Ecological Statistics (EcoStat) team based out of the Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center in Bozeman, MT. EcoStat team led and mentored by experienced collaborative research statistician, Dr. Kathryn M. Irvine. Broadly the EcoStat team engages in applied statistical research motivated by ecological problems relevant to conservation and management of the nation’s natural resources. Research projects are related to modeling spatial and temporally misaligned datasets in order to understand impacts of White-nose syndrome on bat species in the Western United States, research developing and testing statistical models for bat acoustic data, statistical evaluations of long-term, on-going monitoring of ecological indicators in Greater Everglades and beyond, statistical analyses for complex ecological data, and flexible, probability design creation for natural resource agencies.

Project activities include, but are not restricted to, developing and completing rigorous simulation studies to interrogate assumptions underlying statistical inferences stemming from choice of ecological model and monitoring design components, developing and testing novel statistical techniques that overcome inherent gaps in available methodology for analyzing real-world ecological data, creating transferable and reusable code with accessible documentation for practitioners, and/or visualizations of empirical and modeled results for communication with partners.

Project goals and objectives may include peer-reviewed manuscripts, collaborating on the creation and development of USGS software releases, and/or presenting novel research at professional meetings and conferences.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will gain experience within a premier natural science research agency and participating in large collaborative science teams. You will learn effective strategies for communicating with diverse science domain experts with varying levels of statistical training, techniques for conveying and explaining complex statistical information for non-statistical researchers, statistical collaboration skills with federal and state agency scientists, and how to pace projects and develop achievable milestones that demonstrate effective applied statistical practice. You are expected to be trained and become highly competent in statistical and data science skills (specific to your level of education) and the ability to communicate knowledge gaps early and acquire necessary technical skills independently and efficiently. 

Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Kathryn Irvine ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research please contact the mentor.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of DOI and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

Participants do not become employees of USGS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Experience or clear interest in ecological applications

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), located in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: The Risk Assessment Support Division within the United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP) focuses on developing the tools, approaches and data needed to modernize chemical risk assessment and foster the incorporation of more efficient, non-traditional toxicity testing strategies into regulatory decision making. Currently, scientists in the RASD are engaged in multi-year collaborative projects across the agency with a common goal of these projects being to use in vitro new approach methodologies (NAMs), specifically high-throughput profiling assays, to characterize the biological activity of chemicals in either human or non-human cell types and use that information to inform chemical risk assessment.

To date, two high-throughput profiling assays have been established at the U.S. EPA 1) imaging-based high-throughput phenotypic profiling (HTPP) using the Cell Painting assay and 2) high-throughput transcriptomics (HTTr) using targeted RNA-Seq. These assays are compatible with multiple human and non-human derived cell types. These assays provide information on many different toxicologically relevant biological targets and cellular processes that can be affected by chemicals. You will gain experience being part of the design, conducting and analyzing multiple chemical screening studies performed in human cell lines using these high-throughput profiling assays.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn to:

Culture human cell lines.
Design and conduct high-throughput chemical bioactivity screens using laboratory automation.
Execute high-throughput chemical screening experiments using HTPP and HTTr
Apply computational concentration-response modeling and profile similarity approaches to analyze and interpret high-throughput profiling data.
Synthesize results for publications and presentations.
Participatory activities and opportunities for gained experience include:

Hands-on participation in experimental research in a toxicology laboratory setting.
Building experience in computational toxicology approaches by leading data analysis efforts.
Active participation in project team, branch and division meetings.
Preparing presentations, internal reports and data summaries.
Presenting at scientific conferences.
Co-authoring manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Clinton Willis ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Fall/Winter 2026. All start dates are flexible and vary depending on numerous factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

EPA Security Clearance: Completion of a successful background investigation by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is required for an applicant to be on-boarded at EPA.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and EPA. Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5 year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received a bachelor's or master's degree in the one of the relevant fields (biology, toxicology, biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics, bioinformatics, computational biology, computational chemistry, chemistry, or a related field). Degree must have been received within the past five years.

Preferred skills:

Cell culture experience (e.g., plating, maintaining, freezing animal cells using aseptic technique)
Experience with microscopy (bright field, phase contrast, fluorescence, confocal)
Previous experience with high content imaging datasets
Previous experience with transcriptomics datasets
Computational skills (e.g., programming, R-based statistics)
Courses in biostatistics and/or bioinformatics
Familiarity with literature search tools and strategies
Skills in oral and written communication
Previous research experience, beyond lab-oriented courses alone

Regular, Full-Time, RCUH Non-Civil Service position with the Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit (PCSU), Hawai‘i Ant Lab (HAL), located in Hilo, Hawai‘i. Continuation of employment is dependent upon program/operational needs, satisfactory work performance, availability of funds, and compliance with applicable Federal/State laws. 

MONTHLY SALARY RANGE:  $6,266.06 - $7,000/Mon. 

DUTIES:  Manages the invasive ant strategy for Hawai‘i and the daily research and extension program of the Hawai‘i Ant Lab (HAL), including fiscal and human resource management.  The program’s mission is to protect agriculture, people, and the environment of Hawai‘i from the introduction of new invasive ants, to prevent or reduce the spread of existing ant species, and to eradicate infestations where this is feasible.  Accomplishes this by developing and implementing a comprehensive strategy that minimizes impacts associated with the threat of invasive ants and promotes biosecurity collaboration within the Pacific region.  Expected outcomes of the program include enhanced awareness of invasive ant issues and development of new and novel solutions to control invasive species for people, industry, and natural resource managers. Directs, supervises, and assigns work to Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit (PCSU) HAL staff. Drives to meetings and to the field in UH trucks. 

PRIMARY QUALIFICATIONS:
EDUCATION: Master’s Degree from an accredited college or university in Biology, Entomology, or a conservation related field. (Bachelor’s Degree from an accredited four (4) year college or university in Biological Sciences, Natural Resources Management, or related field with two (2) years of graduate training or project management experience may be substitute for a Master’s Degree.).
EXPERIENCE: Three to five (3-5) years of experience related to job duties. Experience must include at least two (2) years of research experience in invertebrate biosecurity or invasive ant research and two (2) years of experience managing research teams in a high-performing environment, policy development, and strategic planning. A successful track record of grant acquisition and management with proven experience in the development of new technologies.
KNOWLEDGE: Working knowledge of invasive ant biology, biosecurity procedures, state and federal legislation relating to these fields, policy development, and strategic planning. Extensive knowledge of pesticides, mode of action, and formulation of pesticide products. Thorough working knowledge of culture in Hawai‘i and the Pacific region is required. Knowledge of various avenues for gathering technical and legislative information. Knowledge of management principles including, but not limited to, supervising/developing employees, EEO, workplace safety, corrective/disciplinary actions, and administration of policies and procedures.
ABILITIES & SKILLS: Demonstrated ability to foster teamwork with a wide range of people and mentor subordinate staff. Proven ability to produce tangible outcomes, manage multiple projects, and work well under deadlines. Skilled in use of electronic communications and word processing, spreadsheet, and statistical software. Excellent oral and written communication and organizational skills. Strong interest in the protection of Hawai‘i’s natural resources and in innovative solutions to the problem of harmful non-native species invasion. Ability to work normal weekday business hours and occasional evenings and weekends, and to travel on short notice. Ability to establish work standards/expectations and clear direction to meet goals and objectives of ongoing work for direct reports.  Ability to provide guidance, motivate, and engage direct reports through effective communication and leadership.  Ability to assign work and to establish work rules and acceptable levels of quality and quantity of work.  Ability to review work and evaluate performance, and develop required job competencies of direct reports. Must possess a valid driver’s license (and if use of personal vehicle on the job is required, must also have valid personal driver’s insurance equivalent to Hawai‘i’s No-Fault Driver’s Insurance) and maintain throughout the duration of employment. Post Offer/Employment Condition: Must be able to pass a post offer criminal background check. Must complete the online Hazard Communication training immediately after hire or no later than employee’s initial exposure to hazardous chemicals.
POLICY/REGULATORY REQUIREMENT: As a condition of employment, employee will be subject to all applicable RCUH policies, procedures, and trainings and, as applicable, subject to University of Hawai‘i's and/or business entity's policies, procedures, and trainings.  Violation of RCUH's, UH's, or business entity's policies and/or procedures or applicable State or Federal laws and/or regulations may lead to disciplinary action (including, but not limited to possible termination of employment, personal fines, civil and/or criminal penalties, etc.). 

SECONDARY QUALIFICATIONS:    
Possess a Hawai‘i class nine or ten (9 or 10) pesticide applicator’s license. Experience in management or administration of a research project at the post-secondary education level. Working knowledge of RCUH policies and procedures.

Job Title: Forest Manager

Location: Hawai‘i Island

About Forest Solutions:

Forest Solutions Inc. (FSI) has been Hawaiʻi’s leading forestry and land management company for over 30 years, specializing in large-scale tree planting, invasive species control, wildfire prevention, native forest restoration, timber plantation management, forest inventory, agroforestry, permitting, and community engagement. We help Hawaiʻi Grow! 

As a team-oriented small business, FSI brings together project managers, foresters, natural resource specialists, technicians, and field crews to address Hawaiʻi’s unique land management challenges. Our work is rooted in scientific best practices, field expertise, and a deep connection to Hawaiʻi’s biocultural heritage. FSI has played a key role in shaping large-scale forest management, including supporting active management of over 500,000 acres per year and planting over 1,000,000 native plants across more than 5,000 acres, including the largest native forest restoration project in the state.

This is an opportunity to be part of a diverse and impactful team working on meaningful conservation efforts in Hawaiʻi’s stunning and rugged landscapes.

About the Job:

We are seeking a versatile Forest Manager to oversee end-to-end operations across our forestry, wildfire mitigation and fuel reduction, vegetation management, ecological restoration, and natural resource projects across Hawaiʻi. This is a full-time, year-round position with supervisory responsibilities. Reporting to a Senior Forester, this position bridges technical project administration and hands-on operational side of natural resource management. The candidate will be expected to take projects from initial planning and proposal development through budgeting, scheduling, field implementation, monitoring, reporting, and client communication. The position requires someone who can independently manage multiple projects at once while coordinating field crews, subcontractors, landowners, agencies, and other project partners.

This position requires someone who thrives in a highly variable environment, with roughly 60% of your time spent outdoors in variable weather and 40% in the office. Field conditions often involve remote off-road driving, cross-country hiking sometimes 10+ miles off trail, navigating thick rain forests as well as dry, hot environments, and conducting quality control checks across projects ranging from small parcels to landscape-scale efforts spanning tens of thousands of acres. Office time is reserved for GIS/drone data processing, supply procurement, maintenance logging, taking client & internal meetings, budgeting, proposal creation, and project planning and reporting. Work is project-based and highly responsive to client needs and timelines. Schedule flexibility, a sense of purpose, and self-motivation are essential, in addition to technical skills. 

The work location is variable on Hawaiʻi Island. Due to emergency response needs, the candidate must reside on or relocate to Hawaiʻi Island. The day-to-day locations can change as our client mix and project priorities change. We have projects throughout Hawaiʻi Island, and a few on the other Hawaiian Islands, and help each other out when needed. Occasional travel should be expected.


Candidate Selection Criteria:

Candidates will be evaluated for Entry, Mid, or Senior placement based on their background and professional experience in forestry, natural resource management, environmental science, conservation biology, ecology, wildlife management, or a related field.

Description
Please note: Applications will be accepted through 11:59 p.m. MDT on the posting end date. 

The Idaho Department of Fish and Game (IDFG) is seeking a Regional Technical Assistance Manger to fill our current opening at our Clearwater Regional Office in Lewiston. 

The Regional Technical Assistance Manager is a critical component of the Regions Management team working in conjunction with the Regional Supervisor and Regional Fish, Wildlife, Habitat, Communications and Enforcement Managers. The position manages all technical assistance requests and responses to and from the region. The position also works closely with the Technical Services Bureau and is a member of the Statewide Technical Assistance Program. 

If you enjoy influencing the conservation and management of fish and wildlife resources, working with people with diverse interests, collaborating with local, state and Federal agencies, have a knack for critical thinking, good knowledge of fish and wildlife biology and management practices, strong team and problem-solving skills, and willing to provide excellent customer service; the Regional Technical Assistance Manager is the job for you! 

Why IDFG? We are a premier natural resource agency dedicated to preserving, protecting, perpetuating, and managing Idaho's fish and wildlife for this great state. We are committed to creativity, innovation, and excellence as we cultivate opportunities for our customers to engage with our natural resources and become resource stewards for future generations. We are highly dedicated to our mission, committed to our team, and we know how to balance work/life commitments while loving the work we do. 

What We Offer:  

Excellent medical, dental, and vision insurance - employee only coverage for PPO $70.74/month for medical and vision & $12.08/month for dental
Participation in one of the Nation's best state retirement systems
Generous vacation and sick leave accrual that begins as soon as you start (accumulate approximately 3 weeks of vacation the first year, and increasing with state longevity)
Eleven paid holidays a year
Eight weeks of Paid Parental Leave
Multiple saving plans-optional 401k and 457 plans 
Group Life Insurance/Disability Insurance/Supplemental Life Insurance - state provided basic life insurance coverage and affordable supplemental plans 
Public Sector Student Loan Forgiveness (eligibility requirements may apply)
Employee Assistance Program - confidential support, information, and resources for all of life's challenges
State and Department Wellness Programs 
Ongoing training opportunities
Potential flexible work schedule  

Responsibilities:
This position's responsibilities include assessing proposed management and development actions on fish and wildlife and their habitats. The successful applicant will be responsible for being familiar with site-specific fish and wildlife conditions and proposals, understanding the ecological and biological ramifications of management actions on fish and wildlife and their habitats, and effectively communicating both orally and in writing the management effects, alternatives, and proposed mitigation to agencies, professionals, and the public. Management actions most commonly evaluated include land use plans, residential development, stream alterations, industrial and commercial developments, water rights, vegetation management including timber harvest, livestock grazing, and prescribed fire, hydropower licensing, energy and mineral extraction proposals and ongoing projects, and transportation plans and developments. The Regional Technical Assistance Manger position is responsible for effectively coordinating with other IDFG staff, is the Idaho Fish and Wildlife Information System (IFWIS) point of contact for IDFG at the regional level and is the primary natural resource person for the Regional Supervisor on all issues effecting fish and wildlife resources and related recreational activities. The position coordinates regional responses very closely with the Technical Services Bureau.

Minimum Qualifications:
(All qualifications listed below are required. To be considered for this position, applicants must meet the minimum experience and/or education standards as outlined in each of the typical qualification guidelines. A detailed resume or work history must be submitted, clearly demonstrating/supporting how you meet each requirement. This information is essential to our initial evaluation process. Incomplete applications or those lacking relevant details may not be considered for further review.) 

Experience demonstrating good knowledge of fish, wildlife, conservation biology, plant ecology and/or habitat management practices. (Typically gained by successful completion of a Master's Degree in Fisheries, Wildlife, or Natural Resource Management from an accredited college or university and at least two years of professional experience such as habitat and resource management or fish and wildlife population management OR successful completion of a Bachelor's Degree in Fisheries, Wildlife, or Natural Resource Management from an accredited college or university and at least four years of professional experience such as habitat and resource management or fish and wildlife population management OR at least eight years of professional experience such as habitat and resource management or fish and wildlife population management.)
Experience evaluating the impact of land use practices and natural processes on habitats, developing, and interpreting statistical data and formulas used in biological research. (Typically gained by at least two years of professional work experience providing input into these areas.)
Experience evaluating and interpreting environmental documents, state and federal regulations, and providing a written and oral analysis of findings. (Typically gained by at least two years of professional work experience providing input on methodology, gathering, and analyzing wildlife data, and providing written and oral analysis of findings. Field research in a wildlife management-related master's degree thesis program is typical at this level.) 

Minimum Qualification Specialty Area: (The qualification listed below is an additional qualification that is required for the current opening at the Idaho Department of Fish and Game.) 

Experience working with state and federal natural resource agencies and associated environmental laws. (Typically gained by at least two years of professional experience working with state and federal natural resource agencies and associated environmental laws and associated environmental laws.)

Job Title: Operations Forester
